hello.note: Literally 'I see you'; to a group say Sanibonani (sah-nee-boh-NAH-nee).

good_evening.note: Built the same way as Sawubona ekuseni; ntambama covers late afternoon into evening, so native speakers also hear this as 'good afternoon'.

goodbye.note: Said by the one leaving; the one staying replies Hamba kahle (HAHM-bah KAH-hleh), 'go well'.

how_are_you.note: To more than one person: Ninjani? (nee-n-JAH-nee).

no_problem.note: Literally 'it is fine'; the all-purpose reply to thanks.

please.note: Literally 'I ask/request'; tacked onto the front of a request.

excuse_me.note: The x is a click: press the tongue to the side teeth and pull it down sharply, like the sound used to call a horse. Respellings here use kh, hl, etc. only to hint at the mouth shape; a native speaker's click will sound sharper.

sorry.note: More formal apology than Uxolo; fine for real mistakes, not just minor bumps.

no.note: The c is a dental click, tongue tip off the top teeth, close to an English 'tsk'.

amazing.note: From -mangala, 'to be astonished'; a warm way to say something blew you away.

delicious.note: Also just means 'nice/pleasant'; the go-to compliment for a cook.

cheers.note: A festive shout of celebration ('hooray!/congratulations!'), said when raising a glass; there is no literal Zulu 'clink' word, so this is the natural stand-in for Western 'Cheers!'.
